description: No genuine fox nature-spirit is documented in Haida tradition; this entry is an unverifiable composite. Haida cosmology centers on Raven as trickster and creator, the Bear Mother, the supernatural killer-whale beings Sgaana, and the culture hero Nanasimget, none of which includes a fox spirit.
source: Not independently attested; no Haida source documents a fox spirit (cf. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths)
research_notes: Not independently attested. Web research found no Haida fox spirit; the entry matches the AI-generated 'X nature-spirit of [nation]' cluster. Genuine Haida beings: Raven, Bear Mother, Sgaana (killer whales), Nanasimget.

description: No fox messenger spirit is attested in Creek (Muscogee) tradition. Documented Muscogee supernatural beings include Chufi, the Rabbit trickster; Kolowa, a hairy man-eating ogre; the underwater Tie-snakes; and Isti Papa, the 'man-eater' giant. The entry invents a messenger role with no support in ethnography.
source: Not independently attested; Muscogee (Creek) oral tradition and ethnographic records
research_notes: Not independently attested. Creek/Muscogee lore documented at native-languages.org and in Muskogean ethnography lists Chufi, Kolowa, tie-snakes, Isti Papa — no fox spirit or fox messenger.

description: In Choctaw tradition the hawk is honored for its keen sight and hunting prowess, qualities tied to vision and perception. Choctaw cosmology holds that each person carries a shilup (soul or spirit) and that the natural world is filled with spirit beings. The hawk figures as a symbol of sharp perception; the historic Choctaw homeland was the forested Southeast, not desert or prairie.
source: Choctaw oral tradition; Native American ethnography (Swanton, Mooney)
research_notes: Attested as a hawk spirit of vision/insight in Choctaw belief. Original description's 'protector of the deserts and prairies' is geographically wrong — the Choctaw homeland is the forested Southeast.

description: No hawk ghost is documented in Ute tradition. Ute oral traditions concern the culture hero Sinawav and spirit beings tied to their Great Basin and Plateau homelands, but no spectral hawk guardian of canyons or springs appears in published ethnography. The entry appears to be an invented composite of generic motifs.
source: Not independently attested; Ute oral tradition and published ethnography
research_notes: Not independently attested. Searches of Ute folklore found no hawk ghost; the specific White Mesa, springs, and petroglyph framing is unsupported.

description: No hawk trickster appears in Paiute tradition; the trickster of the Great Basin peoples, including the Paiute, is Coyote, often malevolent, lecherous, and sometimes a fire-bringer. No source documents a hawk in that role, and the entry's meditation on 'questioning received wisdom' is invented.
source: Not independently attested; Paiute and Great Basin oral tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. Great Basin trickster is Coyote among Paiute, Chemehuevi, Shoshone, and Ute; no hawk trickster documented.

description: In Kikuyu (Kenya) oral tradition, the hawk and the chameleon act as the messengers of Ngai, the supreme god, in the myth that explains the origin of death: the chameleon's delayed return made mortality permanent. This is a genuine Kikuyu belief mislabeled as a USA deity; the Kikuyu homeland is central Kenya.
source: Kikuyu (Gikuyu) oral tradition; Kenyan ethnography
research_notes: Attested as Kikuyu. Entry country/culture metadata (United States/USA) is wrong — origin is Kenya (Kikuyu); the 'diaspora communities' framing in the original was invented.

description: No Khmer hawk spirit is attested; the entry's narrative of a 'Canada mythology' hawk guiding Cambodian immigrants is invented. In Cambodian tradition the principal avian supernatural figure is Garuda, drawn from Hindu-Buddhist syncretism, not a hawk spirit.
source: Not independently attested; Cambodian (Khmer) tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. Original text is a fabricated migration metaphor; genuine Khmer avian being is Garuda (Hindu-Buddhist).

description: No Khmer hawk spirit is attested in Cambodia or diaspora traditions; the text is a near-duplicate of the Canada entry, repeating an invented immigration narrative and copy-paste errors. The genuine Cambodian avian figure is Garuda of Hindu-Buddhist cosmology.
source: Not independently attested; Cambodian (Khmer) tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. Duplicate of hawkspiritkhmer-canada; both entries repeat the same fabricated text with wrong metadata.

description: The heyoka (heyókȟa) is the sacred clown and contrary of Lakota tradition, a role taken only by those who have dreamed of the thunder-beings, Wakíŋyaŋ. Heyokas act backwards and use satire and shocking behavior to mirror a community's doubts, fears, and vanities, functioning as social critics and spiritual teachers who maintain balance.
source: Lakota spiritual tradition; Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual
research_notes: Attested. Core description accurate; 'serves as' phrasing removed. Heyoka role requires a vision of the Wakíŋyaŋ (thunder beings).

description: The wendigo (windigo, witiko) is a malevolent cannibal spirit of Algonquian peoples — Ojibwe, Cree, Innu, Naskapi, and Algonquin — not the Huron, whose traditions the entry wrongly implies. Documented first by Paul Le Jeune in 1636, the wendigo is an emaciated, ice-hearted giant whose insatiable hunger warns against greed, isolation, and cannibalism in the winter woods.
source: Algonquian folklore; Jesuit Relations (Paul Le Jeune, 1636)
research_notes: Attested. Wendigo is Algonquian-wide, not Huron/Wendat; slug's 'huron' prefix is a misattribution. First written mention 1636 by Paul Le Jeune.

description: The jack ball is a protective charm of African American Hoodoo and conjure: a red-flannel bundle of roots, herbs, bones, coins, nails, and personal objects bound with string, dressed with oils and 'fed' to maintain its power. Placed to guard a home or carried as a talisman, it descends from Kongo nkisi power objects and parallels the mojo bag.
source: African American Hoodoo and conjure tradition; Charles C. Jones, Negro Myths from the Georgia Coast (1888)
research_notes: Attested. Genuine conjure charm; Kongo nkisi connection and mojo-bag parallel are accurate.

description: Kalga Jaad (Ice Woman) is a supernatural being of Haida tradition, counted among the Sgaana Kiidads and appearing in the Raven Traveling narratives recorded by John R. Swanton. She commands ice and winter storms, pairing with Gaayhllga Jaad (Flood-Tide Woman) to represent the balance of seasonal forces in Haida cosmology.
source: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905)
research_notes: Attested. Matches Swanton's Haida supernatural beings; 'embodies the' phrasing removed.

description: In Blackfoot tradition the Medicine Pipe came to the people through a supernatural encounter: a woman appeared to a fasting man with a pipe adorned with eagle feathers and its prayers, or the Thunder spirit delivered it where lightning struck. The pipe mediates between humans and the spirit world, and its keeper observes strict taboos and yearly renewal ceremonies.
source: Blackfoot (Siksika) oral tradition; George Bird Grinnell
research_notes: Attested. Medicine Pipe origin story documented by Grinnell; both the woman-giver and Thunder-giver versions are recorded.

description: Skan (Taku Skanskan) is the sky spirit and supreme judge in Lakota cosmology as recorded by James R. Walker. Born of the waters that Inyan could not hold, Skan sets motion and law for all things, arbitrates among the four primary Wakan Tanka spirits, and judges souls after death. He is associated with the blue of the sky.
source: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual
research_notes: Attested. Walker's account is the primary written source; scholars note Walker's reconstructions should be read critically. 'Serves as' phrasing removed.

description: In Hopi creation accounts Sotuknang, nephew and helper of Tawa the Sun Spirit, arranged the universes and brought order from the first world onward. When the third world was destroyed by flood, he guided the righteous into the Fourth World through the sipapu of the Grand Canyon, and he continues as a messenger between Tawa and the people.
source: Hopi oral tradition; anthropological studies of Hopi religion
research_notes: Attested. Original description was truncated mid-sentence; completed and 'serves as' removed. Sotuknang is Tawa's nephew and assistant.

description: Kokyangwuti, Spider Grandmother, is the Earth Goddess and helper of Hopi tradition, partner to Tawa. She created Huzruiwuhti (Woman of Hard Substances), sealed the righteous in hollow reeds during the great flood, guided clans through their migrations, and aided heroes across many Hopi narratives.
source: Hopi oral tradition; anthropological studies of Hopi religion
research_notes: Attested. Original description was truncated; completed and corrected spelling to Kokyangwuti. Flood, migrations, and hero-helper roles are standard.

description: Tsul'kalu, the Slant-Eyed Giant, is the Great Lord of the Game in Cherokee tradition, owner of the wild game of the mountains and master of hunting rites. He dwells on Tanasee Bald in North Carolina at Tsunegûñ'yï; Judaculla Rock bears markings attributed to his hands. His name means 'he has them slanting.'
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee; Cherokee oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Mooney documents Tsul'kalu, Judaculla Rock, and the invisible-giant narrative; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: Wasgo, the Sea Wolf, is a Haida supernatural being combining wolf and killer-whale features — wolf head and body with the fins and tail of a whale. A crest figure for Haida clans, he crosses between ocean and forest worlds, and his stories teach the fluid boundaries between animal beings in the Haida worldview.
source: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905)
research_notes: Attested. Swanton records Wasgo as wolf-whale hybrid crest being; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: The boggart is a mischievous and often malevolent household spirit of northern English folklore, especially Lancashire and Yorkshire, that hides objects, spoils food, and makes night noises to torment a family. Tied to a house rather than a person, it is hard to drive away; flaxseed scattering or moving house may fail, as the boggart can follow.
source: Northern English folklore; Lancashire and Yorkshire oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Standard boggart lore (object-hiding, flaxseed-counting, following when families move); original text was trimmed to the 150-400 char range.

description: No ant spirit or ant atua is attested in Maori tradition; the entry's narrative of a forest-guardian ant is invented. Maori supernatural beings include the patupaiarehe, pale-skinned fairy folk of forest and mountain, the maero, and the taniwha, water guardians — none of which is an ant.
source: Not independently attested; Maori (Aotearoa New Zealand) oral tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. Genuine Maori forest/water beings are patupaiarehe, maero, and taniwha; the kaitiaki framing is real but no ant spirit or ant atua exists.

description: Anulap is the god of knowledge and magic in the mythology of Chuuk (Truk) in the Federated States of Micronesia, husband of the creator goddess Ligobubfanu and grandfather of the trickster Olifat. He taught humanity navigation, medicine, and sacred arts, and his wisdom was essential to voyagers reading stars, currents, and winds between the islands.
source: Chuukese (Micronesian) mythology; regional ethnographic accounts
research_notes: Attested. Chuuk Anulap with Ligobubfanu and Olifat is consistent with Micronesian sources; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: Bulyit is a Noongar (southwestern Australian) name for small, hairy, malevolent spirit-beings — grouped with Gnardi and Mumari — that lurk in shadows and are said to carry off children who stray from camp, especially near sundown. The entry misattributes them to the Wurundjeri and Kulin nations of Victoria; the term is genuinely Noongar.
source: Noongar (Nyungar) oral tradition; Wikimedia Incubator Wp/nys records; Gerhardt Laves field recordings
research_notes: Attested but mislocated. Bulyit (with Gnardi, Mumari) is Noongar, southwestern Western Australia, not Wurundjeri/Kulin (Victoria) as the entry claims.

description: No butterfly spirit or guardian of sacred mountains is attested in Tongan tradition; Tongan mythology centers on Maui, the sky and sea god Tangaloa, and the divine descent of the royal lineage. The entry's description is an invented nature-spirit narrative with no documentary basis.
source: Not independently attested; Tongan mythology and oral tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. No Tongan butterfly being found in sources; genuine Tongan mythology is Maui, Tangaloa, and divine royal ancestors.

description: Julunggul (Yurlunggur) is the Rainbow Serpent of the Yolngu people of Arnhem Land, a creator being of the Gunapipi ceremony who controls the monsoon and the waters. He swallows and regurgitates initiates to symbolize death and rebirth, and he can bring life-giving rain or destructive floods when angered.
source: Yolngu oral tradition; Arnhem Land ethnography (Ronald Berndt, Gunapipi)
research_notes: Attested. Julunggul/Yurlunggur of the Yolngu and Gunapipi rites is well documented; 'embodies the' phrasing removed.

description: Kamapua'a, the 'hog child,' is a Hawaiian kupua, a demigod of dual human and pig nature, born on Oahu to Hina and the chief Kahikiula. Associated with Lono and agriculture, he is defiant and untamed, famous for his shapeshifting between human, hog, fish, and plant forms and for his stormy pursuit of the fire goddess Pele.
source: Hawaiian oral tradition and folklore collections
research_notes: Attested. Kamapua'a as pig-god kupua, Lono association, and Pele conflict are standard; 'embodies the' phrasing removed.

description: Muldjewangk is a malevolent water spirit of the Murray River region in Aboriginal tradition, dwelling in deep pools and the lower Murray and Lake Alexandrina. It capsizes boats and drags the unwary under, and the stories warn children against swimming alone in deep waters while some accounts cast it as guardian of the river's secrets.
source: Aboriginal Australian oral tradition, Murray River region
research_notes: Attested. Muldjewangk is a documented Murray/lower-lakes water being; cautionary-child-swimming framing accurate; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: Čáhcegearpmaš, also called Vesikäärme, is a water serpent of the Tornedalen region known to Sami and Meänkieli tradition, a close variant of Čáhcerávga, the Northern Sami 'water rávga' — a malevolent water being, shadow of the drowned, that haunts lakes and streams and pulls people, especially children, beneath the surface. The belief remains alive in Sami-language media.
source: Sami oral tradition; Samimuseum.fi; Samer.se; Sveriges Radio Manaidradio (2024)
research_notes: Attested as a variant of Cáhcerávga (water rávga), the Sami drowned-spirit. The 'huge serpent guarding fishing spots' framing is a modern children's-radio reading; primary attested form is a shapeshifting water being that drags people under.

description: Lieaibolmmái, the Alder Man, is the Sami god of hunting, archery, and the forest, his name drawn from the alder wood used for bows. He keeps the wild forest animals as his herds and grants or withholds luck in hunting; the bow goddess Juoksáhkká entrusted newborn boys to him so they would become skilled hunters. Offerings ensured success after reindeer, elk, and small game.
source: Sami religion sources; Ganander (1789); saamelaisensyklopedia.fi
research_notes: Attested. Lieaibolmmái as forest/hunting god, alder-bow etymology, and Juoksáhkká link are documented; 'embodies the' phrasing removed.

description: Rakke is the supernatural dog of the Stallo giant in Sami folklore. If Stallo is slain, Rakke can lick his wounds and restore him to life, so a hero who defeats the giant must also kill the dog or the victory is undone. Rakke appears in the Stallo tales recorded by Qvigstad, including 'How the Stalos Were Tricked.'
source: Sami folklore; Qvigstad recordings; Helgeland Museum
research_notes: Attested. Rakke (Stallo's reviving dog) appears in Qvigstad's Stallo tales; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: No butterfly spirit is attested in Hausa tradition, and the entry is mislabeled as Russian: the Hausa are a West African people. The genuine Hausa spirit world is the bori system of iskoki, organized in the twelve houses of Jangare, but no butterfly iskoki is documented. The description mixes an invented desert-guardian narrative with garbled text.
source: Not independently attested; Hausa bori tradition
research_notes: Not independently attested. Entry wrongly filed under Russia/Slavic; Hausa are West African. Bori iskoki (twelve houses of Jangare) are genuine but no butterfly spirit appears.

description: Kostroma is an East Slavic spring-and-summer fertility figure of Russian folk ritual, honored during Semik as a straw effigy or a disguised girl who is first revered and then burned or drowned to end the season's rites. Her name derives from kostyor, 'bonfire.' The entry's claim that she is a plague goddess is unsupported; her genuine role is seasonal and agricultural.
source: Russian folk ritual; Wikipedia (Kostroma deity); ethnographic records of Semik rites
research_notes: Attested as a Semik fertility/ritual figure. Original 'plague goddess, epidemics, famine' claims are unsupported; name etymology is kostyor (bonfire), not 'straw/stubble'.

description: Krakonoš, known in German as Rübezahl, is the mountain spirit of the Krkonoše (Giant Mountains) on the Czech-Polish border, guardian of the range and its people. He rewards honesty, hard work, and respect for nature while punishing greed and arrogance with wry, inventive retribution; he remains one of the most beloved figures in Czech folklore.
source: Czech and German folklore (Rübezahl tales)
research_notes: Attested. Krakonoš/Rübezahl of the Krkonoše is standard Czech-German folklore; corrected 'Krkonoe' spelling; 'serves as' phrasing removed.

description: No specific Mapuche bear ancestor-spirit is attested; the original description was a copy-paste of the Irish banshee. Genuine Mapuche beings include the ngen, spirit-owners of nature (ngen-kulliñ owns the animals), the Pillan, ancestral volcano and thunder spirits, and the malevolent wekufe.
source: Not independently attested; Mapuche mythology and cosmology
research_notes: Not independently attested. Original description was a verbatim banshee/Bean Sidhe text pasted from an Irish entry. Closest genuine analogues: ngen-kulliñ (animal spirit-owners), Pillan, wekufe.

description: The bear (maskwa) is a powerful medicine being in Cree tradition, a spirit of healing and ceremony and a guide encountered in dreams and visions; legends such as Mistahi-Maskwa tell of a great bear devoted to medicine and the sharing of knowledge. The entry's metadata mislabels the Cree as Colombian, and its lake-guardian framing is unsupported.
source: Cree (Nehiyaw) oral tradition; maskwa medicine teachings
research_notes: Attested as Cree bear medicine spirit (maskwa), but country metadata (Colombia) is wrong — the Cree are Canadian. Specific 'lake guardian' role is unsupported; genuine roles are medicine, ceremony, dreams, and vision guidance.

description: No bison spirit belongs to Guarani tradition: bison never inhabited South America. Guarani cosmology includes the creator Tupa, Arasy, Karai, Jakaira, and the serpent Mboi, but no bison ancestor-spirit. The entry invents a 'sacred bison' narrative that conflates plains-bison symbolism of North America with Guarani beliefs.
source: Not independently attested; Guarani cosmology
research_notes: Not independently attested. Bison are absent from South America. Genuine Guarani figures: Tupa, Arasy, Karai, Jakaira, Mboi (serpent).

description: No Olmec or Brazilian bison trickster exists: bison are absent from Mesoamerica and South America, and the original text itself concedes the figure is not Olmec, describing a fabricated 'South African synthesis.' The entry is a mislabeled invention with no documentary basis.
source: Not independently attested; no source
research_notes: Not independently attested. Original description admits it is not Olmec and invents a 'South African' origin; bison never occurred in Brazil or Mesoamerica.
